passages.original: Tunc loquetur ad eos in ira sua. De ira Dei et Lactantius librum pulcherrimum scripsit, et ipse Origenes creberrime disputat, non tam iram esse, quam necessariam correptionem, ut patris in filium, medici in aegrotum, magistri in discipulum. Ira nu- tem patientibus videri potest, non quod Deus emen- det iratus.
passages.english: Then he will speak to them in his anger. On the anger of God Lactantius also wrote a most beautiful book, and Origen himself argues very often that it is not so much anger as necessary correction, like that of a father toward his son, a physician toward a sick man, a teacher toward his pupil. But it can seem anger to those who suffer it, not that God corrects [them] in anger.

passages.original: Lacum aperuit, etc. Quo eos perderet. Et incidit in foveam quam fecit. In fovea enim mortis quam pa- tefecerat, ipse prior periit : sicut de Ario scriptum est : hoc est, nisi conversi fueritis, nisi egeritis poe- nitentiam, semper diabolus paratum habet arcum, emittit sagittas, quibus nos percutiat. Quorum enim corda ardent libidine, vitiis, et passionibus : isti victi sunt a diabolo. Sagittas suat ardentibus effect. Pulchre dixit, ardentibus : non dixit, arsuris : hoc est, qui arsuri sunt sagittis ipsius : sed quorum- cumque corda ardere viderit, illos perculit. Dicit enim Apostolus ardentes habere diabolum sagittas (Ephes.vi). Ecce parturiit injustitiam, concepit do- lorem, et peperit iniquitatem. Diabolus sic concipit, sic parturit, sic nutrit, sic exaltat. Lacum aperuit, et effodit eum, et incidit in foveam quam fecit. Diabo- lus ipse est lacus, ipse est fovea. Lacum aperuit. Sed quoniam non potest aquam continere secundum Je- remiam : propterea lacus illius versus est in foveam.
passages.english: He has opened a pit, etc. By which to destroy them. And he has fallen into the ditch which he made. For in the ditch of death which he had laid open, he himself perished first, as is written of Arius. That is: unless you are converted, unless you do penance, the devil always has his bow ready; he lets fly arrows with which to strike us. For those whose hearts burn with lust, with vices and with passions: these have been conquered by the devil. He has made his arrows for those who burn. He said well, "for those who burn"; he did not say "for those who will burn", that is, those who are going to be burned by his arrows; but whosoever's hearts he sees burning, those he has struck down. For the Apostle says that the devil has burning arrows (Eph. 6). Behold, he has been in labour with injustice, he has conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity. So the devil conceives, so he is in labour, so he nourishes, so he exalts. He has opened a pit and dug it out, and has fallen into the ditch which he made. The devil himself is the pit, he himself is the ditch. He has opened a pit. But since, according to Jeremiah, it cannot hold water, therefore his pit has been turned into a ditch.
passages.notes: "suat" read as "suas" (scanning error). The lemma "Sagittas suas ardentibus effecit" (Ps. 7:14) is given as "effect" in the scan; read as "effecit".

passages.original: Ego dixi, dii estis, et filii excelsi omnes. Audiat Ennomius, audiat Arius, qui dicunt Filium Dei simi- liter esse filium, ut nos sumus. Quod dii sumus, non est naturae, sed gratiae. Quotquot enim eum recepe- runt, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri (Joan.i). Propterea feci hominem, ut de hominibus dii fiant. Ego dixi, dii estis, et filii excelsi omnes. Videte quan- ta sit dignitas, et dii vocamur et filii. Ego feci vos deos, sicut feci Moysen Pharaonis Deum (Exod.vii) : ut postquam dii fueritis, digni efficiamini filii mei. Considerate Scripturam divinam : Non est persona- rum acceptio apud Deum. Non dixit : Ego dixi, dii estis, reges et principes, sed omnes quibus aequaliter corpus dedi, et animam, et spiritum : aequaliter do- navi, et deitatem, et adoptionem. AEtqualiter omnes nascimur, et imperatores, et pauperes : aequaliter et morimur.
passages.english: I have said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. Let Eunomius hear, let Arius hear, who say that the Son of God is a son in the same way as we are. That we are gods is not of nature but of grace. For as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God (John 1). For this reason I made man, that from men gods might come to be. I have said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. See how great the dignity is: we are called both gods and sons. I made you gods, as I made Moses the god of Pharaoh (Exod. 7), so that after you have become gods you may be made worthy to be my sons. Consider the divine Scripture: There is no respect of persons with God. He did not say: I have said, You are gods, kings and princes; but all, to whom I gave equally body and soul and spirit; equally I have bestowed both deity and adoption. We are all born equally, both emperors and the poor; and equally we die.
passages.notes: "Ennomius" read as Eunomius, the Arian theologian.

passages.original: Qui soloecismos facit in loquendo, crucem Christi portat, et quasi tri- umphans omnes capit. Totum orbem subegit ab Ocea- no usque in mare Rubrum. Dicat aliquis : hoc totum lu- cri causa fecerunt. Hoc enim dicit Porphyrius : Homi- nes rusticani et pauperes, quoniam nihil habebant, ma- gicis artibus operati sunt quaedam signa. Non est au- tem grande facere signa. Nam fecere signa in AEgypto magi contra Moysen (Exod.vii).
passages.english: He who makes solecisms in speaking carries the cross of Christ, and as if triumphing takes everyone captive. He subdued the whole world from the Ocean as far as the Red Sea. Someone may say: they did all this for the sake of gain. For this is what Porphyry says: rustic and poor men, since they had nothing, worked certain signs by magic arts. But it is no great thing to work signs. For the magicians in Egypt worked signs against Moses (Exod. 7).
passages.notes: The subject ("He") is Paul, from the preceding context.

passages.original: Quae Scriptura populis omnibus legitur, hoc est, ut omnes intelligant. Quod dicit, hoc est : Sic- ut scripserunt apostoli, sic et ipse Dominus, hoc est, per Evangelia sua locutus est, non ut pauci in- telligerent, sed ut omnes. Plato scripsit in scriptura, sed non scripsit populis, sed paucis. Vix enim in- tclligunt tres homines. Isti vero, hoc est, principes Ecclesiae et principes Christi, non scripserunt pau- cis, sed universo populo·
passages.english: That Scripture is read to all peoples, that is, so that all may understand. What he says is this: just as the apostles wrote, so the Lord himself also, that is, spoke through his Gospels, not so that a few might understand, but so that all might. Plato wrote in writing, but he did not write for the peoples, but for a few. For scarcely three men understand [him]. But these, that is, the princes of the Church and the princes of Christ, did not write for a few, but for the whole people.

passages.original: Totus hic psalmus est scriptus secundum ordinem litterarum, ita ut ab una litte- ra octo versus incipiant, et rursum a sequenti ocio alii compleantur. Et hoc similiter usque ad finem lexatur. Josephus autem refert in libris αρχαιολογίας hunc psalmum, et Deuteronomii canticum, uno metro esse compositum, et putat elegiacum metrum in utroque posse deprehendi : quod scilicet prior versus sex pedibus conslet, inferior uno minus in pentametrum finiatur.
passages.english: This whole psalm is written according to the order of the letters, so that eight verses begin from one letter, and again eight others are completed from the following [letter]. And this is woven in the same way to the end. Josephus, moreover, reports in the books of the Antiquities that this psalm and the song of Deuteronomy are composed in one metre, and he thinks the elegiac metre can be detected in both: namely, that the first line consists of six feet, and the lower one, one [foot] less, ends as a pentameter.
passages.notes: Scanning errors read: "ocio" as "octo", "lexatur" as "texatur" (woven/continued), "conslet" as "constet". "αρχαιολογίας" = the Jewish Antiquities.
